headToHead.voiceVerdict: Tie. Cover the names on our twelve and the two shapes are Dash's alone: the downward pivot (claim, flinch, smaller claim, cheerful lock-in: rooftop, sorry/agreed, nod, hi) and the calm wrong syllogism (fifth, concert, ahead, postcard). Nobody else in the cast talks like that, and almost none of the twelve needs a startup word to be recognised. But both shapes are mechanical, and once you have heard three of them you can write the fourth; Liam's register (formal clauses on trivia, then a plea) is just as unmistakable and has more range inside it, because the sentence also carries his contradiction. Not a win.
headToHead.constructionVerdict: Ours. Economy is now excellent: full stops, short beats, punch on the last word nearly every time (fifth, concert, rooftop, sleeve, ahead, nod, font, checking). Nothing in the twelve explains itself. Liam's twelve are looser: the time-machine line has no turn, one is a paraphrase, and three are the narrator doing his work for him.
headToHead.quotableVerdict: Bar, narrowly. 'Save me from the consequences of my actions!' and the 360-degree spin get repeated because Liam is wrong about himself and the line shows the dork under the pose. Ours has four genuinely clippable lines (fifth, concert, car-park rooftop, the nice zero), but a clip reel of them is the same joke four times: a bad fact, 'so', a happy conclusion. Liam's quotable lines are each a different way of betraying that he cares; Dash's are one way of not noticing he lost. The only lines where Dash's want shows through on stage are 'Me? On purpose?' and the warm closes, and those are the least jokey in the bank.

templates: Never-never record (6 lines): 'I've never [bad outcome]. I've never [the thing that would let it happen].' plus a tag: 'never lost a final / never reached one. Clean record', 'never been stood up / never told anyone where I'd be', 'never broken a heart / Nobody's ever let me near one. Spotless record', 'never been dumped / never had a second date', 'No one's turned me down twice... then I ask someone new', 'I've never had...' (opener). Nav already owns this exact shape ('I have never been wrong. I have never been near a wedding.'), so it is a cross-cast collision as well as a template.

Leaving is winning (about 9 lines): 'I was going to leave anyway... Compatible', 'I'll tell everyone I left... I'm the one walking', 'Sorry in advance for leaving mid-fight... nobody lost', 'I quit the second something flops... I left before it could', 'Every time I leave a room, people cheer up', 'I'm amazing at ending them' (Tilly roast), 'describe toast to you, from the door', 'Pivoting to the door', 'I'll walk slowly'. Three of the four exit lines are this one joke; a viewer gets it twice per episode at minimum.

Bad perception, so it's going great (4 lines): 'I read every silence as a yes... We're doing great', 'I can't read a room. So every room I'm in is going great', 'I'll tell you how it went. It went great', 'Look at us agreeing'. Same sentence, three wordings.

Count it twice, call it a win (5 lines): 'let me in twice. I'm ahead', 'skipped me twice... Two views', 'he told me. Twice. That's two sources', 'I request it twice, so it's a concert', 'No one's turned me down twice'. The concert is the best of these; the rest dilute it. Number props are also worn: 'four' carries six lines (platforms, exit, four minutes pitched, four-minute songs, four times the songs), 'eleven' two (and Brock says eleven constantly).

Startup-word renames that the persona bans, still present (about 12 lines): ships in March, maintenance mode/never shipped/waitlist, in beta, IPO, shipping a patch/patch notes, hockey stick, supply and demand, pre-revenue/acquisition, pending review, organic/company history, market conditions, strong quarter. Several are good lines (the lilac tie, market conditions, strong quarter) because the turn is elsewhere, but 'It's in beta', 'Hockey stick, babe' and 'supply and demand' are the vocabulary as the joke.

Downward pivot (about 15 lines: rooftop, private jet, pancakes, cut left/right, sorry/agreed, guarded/undecided, nod, strong quarter, moon/balloon, launch party, waitlist, suite/vending machine, one year/engaged, gracious/door, dashboard/you). This is the signature and not counted as generic, but at 13 percent of the bank the scripted brain will serve three or four an episode and it will turn into wallpaper. Cut the weakest three (cut left/right, pancakes, one year).
Same fact per rival twice: Quill's unfinished poem (roast and wingman), Nav's recalculating (roast and jab). The roast, wingman and jab for one rival should be three different observations.

Cross-cast collisions: 'You've checked the exit four times' is Brock's line almost word for word ('You've checked the exit four times and smiled once'); never-never is Nav's shape; 'reference' after a breakup is used by Prince, Tilly and Quill; 'next' in the impression is Pixel's catchphrase; 'vending machine' is in Crumb's and Vex's banks; 'loading' is Pixel's ex and appears in Crumb's and Nav's lines; 'I'm ahead' and 'Two views' sit next to Brock's 'I'm up two smiles' and 'I'm tied with a moth'.
ruleBreaks: Hard limits: none broken. Openers all 12 words or under, jabs 10 or under, three-words exactly 3, every other line 20 or under. No em or en dashes, no emoji, no 'as an AI', no therapy talk, nothing past PG-13, no real people or brands. Exclamation cap of two per line now holds everywhere (r3 had 11 over).

Secret hinted on stage, mild: win line 'Thank you, dashboard! No. Thank you, you.' names the dashboard in public; fine as a win beat, but it is the only on-stage dashboard mention and the persona says never.

Stock romance filler, borderline: 'Pick me tonight and I'll give you the moon!' (rescued by the balloon).

Star side: no cut or reaction to Dash is too nice; every charmed and pick line keeps an edge. Two leftovers: Maximilian charmed 'That converted me. I am billing you for the inconvenience.' still borrows Dash's word, and Maximilian pick 'Tell the dashboard whatever you like.' spoils the secret on stage.
biggestGap: Dash has one joke, the calm wrong syllogism that ends in 'so I'm winning', and it now runs about thirty lines on recycled props (twice, never-never, leaving first), whereas Liam's lines land because the pose cracks inside the sentence and shows how much he cares. In the next pass, rewrite the flagged lines so the airtight wrong conclusion gives away the want instead of the win: he still reasons cheerfully and never sees the flaw, but what he is reasoning toward is being picked on purpose (the 'Me? On purpose? Nobody clicked anything by accident?' kind), so the clip is of a man who badly needs this, not a man spinning a loss.

notes: Corpus file present and read in full, with charm-notes.md, CAST.md, the Dash persona, the full Dash bank (112 lines), the three star banks' Dash entries, and the seven rival suitor banks for collisions. Bar twelve are verbatim from refs/writing/monster-prom-lines.md; Liam kept as the job match (a self-image he cannot live up to, 'hype', 'disruptive', confident wrong reasoning), though four of his twelve are narrator, paraphrase or player lines, which flatters our construction score. Real progress since r3: exclamation cap now holds on every line, the jargon swap is down from about 20 lines to about 12, the countdown lists are gone bar one, and the downward pivot and the syllogism both read as Dash with the name covered. The generic share is flat at 35 percent only because new templates grew where the old ones were cut: never-never (which collides with Nav), leaving-as-winning (three of four exits), and count-it-twice. Fastest wins: replace 'You've checked the exit four times' (Brock's line), keep only one never-never line (the final/'Clean record' opener is the best of them), keep one exit about leaving and make the others about something else, and give each rival three different facts across roast, wingman and jab.
